newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arabs and Israel -- Who's talking, who's trading.
newsitem.headline: Arabs and Israel -- Who's talking, who's trading.

text.p: Here is an outline of the state of contacts established between Israel and Arab states in the three years since Israel and the Palestinians reached their first agreement.
An Arab League resolution passed on Monday recommends that Arab states suspend normal relations with Israel and restore the economic boycott.

Countries which have signed formal agreements with the Jewish state -- Egypt, Jordan and the Palestinians -- are exempt from the full force of the resolution but they too might take steps to minimise contacts with Israelis. -- COUNTRIES COVERED BY THE ARAB LEAGUE RESOLUTION --

MAURITANIA - Mauritania and Israel signed a mutual recognition pact in Spain in November 1995 and Israel opened a special interest section at the Spanish embassy in Nouakchott in June 1996. Mauritania has a similar office in Tel Aviv.

MOROCCO - King Hassan of Morocco was a pioneer, behind the scenes, in contacts with Israeli leaders, even before Egypt made peace with the Jewish state in 1979, but formal arrangements had to wait for the Israeli-Palestinian agreement of 1993.

In 1994 Morocco and Israel opened low-level diplomatic links through liaison bureaus in each country. The current head of the Israeli bureau, David Dadonn, said the volume of trade in 1994 and 1995 was several tens of millions of dollars a year.
"There is scarcely a week when there is not a Moroccan businessman or delegation in Israel," he added.

Dadonn said the last visit by a senior Israeli took place last August, when opposition leader and former prime minister Shimon Peres visited the country. But at lower diplomatic levels, contacts remain frequent, he added.

OMAN - Oman has forged ahead with establishing economic ties with Israel after the 1993 peace accord. Last August it became the first Gulf Arab country to have any representation in Israel after opening a commercial bureau in Tel Aviv. Israel has also set up a similar office in Muscat.
Netanyahu's policies have put a damper on Muscat's enthusiasm and it has recently joined a chorus of condemnation of Israel by the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).
On March 23, Oman said it had frozen ties with Israel over the Jewish state's settlement policies.
At the Arab League meeting, the Omani foreign affairs minister said his country would "most probably" close the representative office in Israel "when necessary".
QATAR - Qatar was the other Gulf Arab state which hastened to set up ties with Israel but it has also stopped short of establishing diplomatic relations until there is full peace.
Israel has set up a trade office in Doha but Qatar said it would not proceed with its plan to open a trade mission in Israel until there was progress in peace talks.
Qatar is also a member of the GCC and its foreign minister said in Cairo that his country would abide by any Arab League resolution calling for halting contacts with Israel.

TUNIS - Israel formally opened an interest bureau in Tunis in April 1996 and a month later, Tunisia -- home of the Palestinian Liberation Organisation for several years -- set up a five-person office in a Tel Aviv hotel.
In December, and in response to Netanyahu's settlement policies, Tunis said its ties with Israel were put on hold and contacts with the representative office practically stopped.

Officials do not report any trade with the Jewish state but businessmen in both countries have established discreet ties. Last June, a group of private Tunisian businessmen -- including the son-in-law of President Zine al-Abidine Ben Ali -- went on the first publicised visit to Israel.

On the official level, the friendly ties between King Hassan and the former Labour government did not extend to Netanyahu. The monarch sent Netanyahu only one public message after Israel agreed to redeploy from the West Bank town of Hebron.
-- COUNTRIES NOT COVERED BY THE ARAB RESOLUTION --
EGYPT - Egypt became the first Arab country to make peace with Israel after signing the Camp David treaty in 1979.
But ties with the Jewish state have remained cool on the official level and many Egyptians still remain hostile to the longstanding enemy they fought in four regional wars.

In 1981, former president Anwar Sadat was slain by Moslem militant gunmen for making peace with Israel. His successor Hosni Mubarak, now in his 16th year in power, has not advanced relations with the Jewish state beyond the formal.
Ties became strained after Netanyahu's election and then even more so after Egypt said it would put on trial an Israeli suspected of espionage. Israel says the man is not a spy.

The countries mistrust each other's intentions. Israel has charged Egypt, which regards itself an unofficial sponsor of the peace process and which usually champions the Palestinians, of being biased. Mubarak on his part says Israel is not keeping its word and implementing the peace deals it signed.

Trade between the two states in not substantial but Egypt exports crude oil to Israel and there is official cooperation in agriculture. A handful of private sector businessmen have ties with the Jewish state, the most prominent being Egyptian tycoon Ibrahim Kamel, who bought a stake in Israel's Koor Industries.
JORDAN - Although Jordan signed a peace treaty with Israel only three years ago, its contacts with the Jewish state have gone much further than any other Arab country.
King Hussein suprised the Arab world with his deep friendship with assassinated Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin and he continues to have overtly good ties with Netanyahu.

Officials cite Jordan's role in brokering the January accord on Israel's withdrawal from Hebron as vindication of its policy of quiet diplomacy, saying only King Hussein enjoyed the trust of Palestinians and Israelis which helped them reach compromise.
Jordan's policy is to keep doors open for dialogue however serious its political differences with the Jewish state. The two countries opened embassies in 1995.
Last year, the volume of trade reached $18 million. In 1996, both states also opened their border to direct trade for the first time in nearly 50 years.

Businessmen say Israelis have set up at least a dozen, mainly low-profile, partnerships in Jordan, most of them in the textile industry. Israelis are also looking at setting up a number of joint venture industries in the Jordan Valley.
